questions.q: What does SCD Type 1 do when a source attribute changes?
options: Overwrites the old value in place, keeping no history of what it used to be
Inserts a brand-new row while keeping the old one unchanged
Adds effective and expiry dates to track when each value was valid
Rejects the change and keeps the original value permanently
questions.explain: SCD1 is the overwrite-in-place strategy — the dimension row reflects only the current state, with no history preserved.

questions.q: What Snowflake statement implements SCD Type 1, and how does its syntax compare to what you already know?
options: MERGE, using the same WHEN MATCHED / WHEN NOT MATCHED structure already familiar from T-SQL
COPY INTO, which is unrelated to updating existing rows
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, which cannot update individual rows
GRANT, which only manages permissions
questions.explain: The MERGE statement's WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE / WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT structure implements SCD1, using the same overall pattern you already know from T-SQL.

questions.q: What is missing from Snowflake's MERGE statement compared to T-SQL's?
options: An OUTPUT clause — there's no way to stream the actual changed rows out of the MERGE statement directly
The WHEN MATCHED clause
The ability to insert new rows
Support for referencing a staging table as the source
questions.explain: Snowflake's MERGE has no OUTPUT clause; Snowsight shows aggregate rows-inserted/rows-updated counts, but individual changed rows aren't streamed out of the statement itself.

questions.q: Why do HASH()-based surrogate keys pair naturally with SCD Type 1?
options: SCD1 never needs to preserve multiple versions of a row, so the key only needs to identify the entity itself, which a HASH of the natural key does directly
HASH() keys are required by Snowflake for any MERGE statement to work
SCD1 cannot use AUTOINCREMENT keys under any circumstances
HASH() keys automatically track historical versions of a row
questions.explain: Because SCD1 has no versioning concept, a deterministic HASH of the natural key is sufficient to identify each row — there's no extra bookkeeping needed for 'which version' the way SCD2 requires.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does SCD Type 1 lose that SCD Type 2 (next lesson) is specifically designed to keep?
options: History of prior attribute values over time
The ability to insert brand-new dimension rows
Support for surrogate keys entirely
The ability to run on a schedule
questions.explain: SCD1's defining trade-off is discarding history on overwrite; SCD2 exists specifically to preserve that history via effective/expiry dating, covered in the next lesson.
